transcript.content: Hello, welcome. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, to be perfectly honest with you, my wife is the main reason I’m sitting here today. We—well, we moved into this condo a few years back after I retired, downsized you know, which was quite a project in itself with all the sorting. But lately, or I suppose for a good while now, I’ve just been having this... this issue when we try to leave the house, or even just when I'm trying to finish a simple morning routine. 

What brought me in is that I find myself checking things. Just the same things, over and over again. It’s the storage boxes in the spare room, my daily task lists, the drawers—especially that little console drawer by the front door where we keep the spare keys and the batteries. I'll check it, and I'll close it, and then I just have to open it and check it again to make sure everything is exactly as I left it. And the lists, oh, I'll read through my lists three, four, five times. I’ll be standing there checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can finally move on to whatever it is I'm supposed to be doing. 

And the ridiculous thing is, I know perfectly well I already looked. My memory is fine, I know exactly what's in there and what's written on the paper. But I just can't seem to walk away until I've looked again. Meanwhile, my wife, she’s standing there by the door with her coat on, holding her purse, just waiting for me to just leave it be so we can go to the grocery store or out to lunch. It drives her absolutely up the wall, and frankly, it's starting to bother me too, because I just get stuck in this loop and it eats up so much time, but if I don't do it, I just can't settle my mind.
When you feel the need to check those things but try to resist doing so, do you experience significant anxiety or discomfort?

Well, yes, absolutely. Anxiety is exactly the word for it, or maybe a sort of buzzing tension, if that makes sense? If I try to just walk away—say I’ve only checked the console drawer once, and I think, "Okay, that's enough, Frank, let's just go"—I get this overwhelming, nagging feeling right in the pit of my stomach. It’s like an itch you can’t scratch, but on the inside. 

I’ll be walking down the hallway toward the front door, and my wife will be saying, "Come on, the car is already warm," but my feet just feel heavy. My mind starts racing, thinking, "Did I really see the spare keys sitting exactly parallel to the batteries? Did I actually read the third item on my list, or did my eyes just skim over it?" And the discomfort just builds and builds. It’s not like I’m afraid the house is going to explode or anything dramatic like that, it’s just this intense, unbearable wrongness. 

Like I was saying earlier, that's the whole reason I'm here. I find myself checking the same boxes in the spare room, those daily lists I make, and those condo drawers over and over before I can move on to the next part of my day. And it’s so frustrating because I know perfectly well I already looked. I know it! But if I try to resist, that awful, tight feeling in my chest just won't let up until I turn around, walk back, and check it all again. And meanwhile, my poor wife is just waiting for me to leave it be, and I can see the patience draining right out of her face, but I just... I can't seem to stop myself without feeling completely out of sorts.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of repetitive checking, distress from resisting the behavior, and associated anxiety strongly point to OCD (F42.2). Other candidates (F43.22, F32.9, F06.4, F07.81) are less consistent with the described behaviors and lack evidence of trauma, mood episodes, or organic factors.

inference_history.note: The patient describes repetitive checking behaviors (e.g., storage boxes, drawers, task lists) accompanied by awareness that these behaviors are excessive and cause distress and time consumption. This presentation primarily suggests a primary obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.2). However, other differential diagnoses are considered, including generalized anxiety disorder (F43.22), major depressive disorder (F32.9) which may present with ruminative behaviors, unspecified obsessive-compulsive disorder (F06.4), and post-retirement adjustment disorder with anxiety (F07.81). Further questioning is needed to clarify the presence of obsessions, the degree of distress, the temporal course, and any associated mood symptoms.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent, intrusive, and distressing urges to perform checking rituals, accompanied by marked anxiety when attempting to resist these behaviors. These symptoms are consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder, specifically with predominantly checking compulsions. The compulsions are aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or distress, rather than preventing an external event, and they are not pleasurable. The behaviors cause clinically significant distress and impairment in daily functioning, particularly in the interpersonal domain with his spouse.
